x3-life-cycle-continuum.title: Appendix X3: continuum of life cycles (predictive, iterative, incremental, agile), iteration-based and continuous overlapping phases
x3-life-cycle-continuum.notes: Explores how the Process Groups are performed across environments and life cycles; the life cycle must be flexible because projects evolve as information becomes available - especially with high change, uncertainty or varied stakeholder expectations. Development life cycles: predictive (plan-driven), adaptive (agile), iterative, incremental, hybrid. Figure X3-1 continuum: Predictive - requirements defined up front before development; deliver plans for the eventual deliverable then a single final product at the end; change constrained as much as possible; key stakeholders involved at specific milestones; risk and cost controlled by detailed planning of mostly knowable considerations. Iterative - requirements elaborated at periodic intervals during delivery; delivery can be divided into subsets; change incorporated at periodic intervals; stakeholders regularly involved; risk and cost controlled by progressively elaborating plans with new information. Incremental - (shares the middle of the continuum with iterative; figure groups iterative/incremental characteristics). Agile - requirements elaborated frequently during delivery; frequent delivery of customer-valued subsets; change incorporated in real time; stakeholders continuously involved; risk and cost controlled as requirements and constraints emerge. Predictive: emphasis on specifying requirements and detailed planning early; M&C focuses on constraining changes to scope, schedule, budget. Agile: progressive elaboration through short planning and executing cycles; continuous stakeholder feedback enables faster response to change and better quality. Middle of the continuum: risk and cost reduced by iterative evolution of plans; more stakeholder involvement opportunities than milestone-based predictive; projects lean predictive or agile depending on requirements, risk/cost handling and stakeholder involvement and may use hybrid methods; different phases of one project (or projects in a program) may use different life cycles. Phases: Process Group processes repeat in each phase until completion criteria are met. Sequential iteration-based phases: adaptive projects decomposed into timeboxed iterations of consistent, pre-agreed duration creating a predictable cadence; repeating Process Groups each iteration adds overhead, accepted for high complexity, uncertainty and change (Figure X3-2: each iteration contains initiating, planning, executing, M&C and closing effort). Continuous overlapping phases: highly adaptive projects perform all Process Groups continuously ('continuous and adaptive planning', inspired by lean); aggressively refine plans beyond iteration checkpoints; continuously pull tasks from a prioritised list, removing iteration start/end overhead - 'microiterations' maximising execution time, still needing their own planning, tracking and adjustment mechanisms (Figure X3-3).

x3-process-groups-adaptive.title: Appendix X3: Process Groups in adaptive environments (initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling via a backlog, closing)
x3-process-groups-adaptive.notes: Initiating: adaptive projects revisit and revalidate the charter frequently because priorities and dynamics may make constraints and success criteria obsolete; rely heavily on a knowledgeable customer or designated customer representative giving continuous feedback - identify them early; an initiating process is typically conducted each iterative cycle. Planning: predictive projects (few scope changes, high stakeholder alignment) benefit from detailed up-front planning; adaptive projects develop high-level plans for initial requirements and progressively elaborate them per planning cycle - they differ in how much planning is done and when; under complexity and uncertainty involve as many team members and stakeholders as possible in planning. Executing: work directed through short fixed iterations ending with a demonstration of functionality or design, then a retrospective with stakeholders and team; demonstrations check progress against plan, decide scope/schedule/process changes and manage engagement; retrospectives surface execution issues and improvements and are a primary tool to manage project knowledge and develop the team; iteration-level trends (development speed, spend, defect rates, team capacity) are summed and extrapolated to track project completion; highly adaptive teams self-organise tasks to meet higher-level objectives rather than the PM selecting and sequencing work - practical plans with high buy-in; junior teams need coaching and assignments first and are reviewed in retrospectives for readiness. Monitoring and controlling: progress regulated through a backlog prioritised by a business representative with the team estimating and flagging technical dependencies; work pulled from the top by business priority and team capacity; change requests and defect reports are evaluated and prioritised into the same backlog - a single list of work and changes that originated where change rates overwhelmed separate change control; this one backlog is where stakeholders manage work, perform change control and validate scope; frequent sampling yields capacity, progress against original scope, change impacts and defect remediation effort, enabling cost, schedule and scope estimates from real rates; shared through trend graphs ('information radiators') to communicate progress, share issues, drive improvement and manage expectations. Closing: highest-value items are done first, so premature closure is likely to have already produced business value - less a sunk-cost failure, more an early benefit realisation, quick win or proof of concept.

x4-x5-summaries.title: Appendices X4 and X5: compiled key concepts and tailoring considerations per Knowledge Area (revision aids)
x4-x5-summaries.notes: X4 compiles the Key Concepts subsections of Sections 4-13 (intended as an aid for practitioners, a checklist of learning objectives for trainers and a study aid for certification candidates); X5 compiles the Tailoring Considerations subsections. Content matches topics already recorded per Knowledge Area (i-key-concepts, s-scope-overview, t-schedule-overview, c-cost-overview, q-quality-overview, r-resource-overview, m-communications-overview, k-risk-overview, p-procurement-overview, h-stakeholder-overview); minor wording differences noted: X4.1 says 'benefits realization plan' where Section 4 says 'benefits management plan'; X4.1 contains a truncated bullet ('The relationships of processes within the Project Management Process Groups and between the Project Management Process') - a source typesetting truncation. X4.5 adds that the most effective quality management incorporates quality into planning and design and an organisational culture committed to quality. Used for the end-of-course revision module and as a cross-check that every Knowledge Area key concept has a lesson objective.

x6-tools-techniques-index.title: Appendix X6: tools and techniques grouped by purpose (132 tools; group counts) and index
x6-tools-techniques-index.notes: Sixth Edition groups tools and techniques by intent - the group names the intent and the members are alternative methods (e.g., data gathering includes brainstorming, interviews, market research) - reflecting the emphasis on tailoring. 132 individual tools and techniques, representing good practice on most projects most of the time (not the only ones possible). Groups and counts: data gathering (collect data and information) - 9; data analysis (organise, assess, evaluate) - 27; data representation (graphic or other methods to convey data) - 15; decision-making (select a course of action) - 2; communication skills (transfer information) - 2; interpersonal and team skills (lead and interact) - 17; plus 60 ungrouped. Table X6-1 indexes each tool by group and the processes using it, with the describing process in bold (bolding is not preserved in extraction). Data gathering rows as extracted: benchmarking (5.2, 8.1, 13.2), brainstorming (4.1, 4.2, 5.2, 8.1, 11.2, 13.1), check sheets (8.3), checklists (4.2, 8.2, 8.3, 11.2), focus groups (4.1, 4.2, 5.2), interviews (4.1, 4.2, 5.2, 8.1, 11.2-11.5), market research (12.1), questionnaires and surveys (5.2, 13.1), statistical sampling (8.3). Source note: some X6 rows do not match the per-process figures (e.g., alternatives analysis listed under 5.4 Create WBS, whose own figure has only expert judgment and decomposition; Define Scope 5.3 uses alternatives analysis) - lessons and questions take tool-to-process mappings from the per-process ITTO figures (ittos.json and the topic notes), using X6 only for the grouping concept and counts.
